summary: For ages 5-7 (Y1/early Y2): solve one-step word problems involving addition and subtraction to 20, including missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9. The core objective is modelling the situation (acting out, drawing, bar/part-whole models) rather than keyword-matching, and crucially handling problems where the unknown sits in the start, change or result position — not only the answer slot. Bar/part-whole models make the unknown visible so children can reason to it using the inverse or a known bond.
misconceptions: Keyword-matching (fails on missing-number and compare problems).
Assuming the unknown is always the result, so start- and change-unknown problems stump them.
Rejecting missing-number forms because = is read as 'answer here'.
Combining the two given numbers regardless of the structure (e.g. adding in a start-unknown problem that needs subtraction).
Not using the inverse/known bond to find the unknown, instead guessing.

activities.title: Story-to-bar-model builder
steps: Listen to or read a one-step problem with numbers to 20, e.g. 'I had some sweets, ate 9, and 7 are left.'
Drag the quantities you know into a bar or part-whole frame — for this story, split a whole into a '9 eaten' part and a '7 left' part.
Mark where the unknown sits in the model (here the WHOLE — the number you started with — is the mystery).
Act on the model to find the unknown — combine the two parts to fill the whole (7 + 9 = 16), or count on along a number line.
Repeat with problems that rotate the unknown through result, change and start positions, and with pure missing-number equations like 7 = ? − 9.
Write the equation that matches your model, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after the = sign).
activities.insight: A problem where the unknown is the START or the CHANGE, not the answer, is not impossible: the bar model shows exactly where the mystery sits. If the unknown is the whole, combining the known parts finds it. If the unknown is a part, taking the known part away from the whole (or counting on from it) finds it. Children learn to model any structure rather than hope a keyword tells them what to do.

activities.title: Hands-on modelling with counters, drawings and paper bars
steps: Act out or draw the story with physical counters before choosing any operation.
Lay out a paper tape/bar strip and partition it into known parts and an unknown part to match the story.
Use an empty number line to count on and find a difference or an unknown.
Say aloud what you know, what you are trying to find, and why the operation you chose fits the story.
activities.insight: Modelling the situation with concrete materials — rather than matching keywords — reveals the correct operation even when the unknown is not the result.

activities.title: Coaching dialogue: 'What do we know, what are we finding?'
steps: Respond to a coach who asks you to name what is known and what is unknown in a problem.
Justify which operation you will use and where the unknown sits, especially for start-unknown and missing-number problems.
Talk through 7 = ? − 9: identify that you need a starting number which, after removing 9, leaves 7.
activities.insight: Reasoning aloud about knowns and the unknown can develop the modelling and inverse reasoning needed for harder problem structures.

activities.title: Worked bar-model example with revealable steps
steps: Study one worked problem shown with a bar model.
Reveal the solution steps one at a time and relate each step to the story.
Restate how the parts and whole map onto what the story gave and what it asked.
activities.insight: A clearly worked bar model anchors the method and shows how the unknown is found from the known quantities: combining the parts when the whole is unknown, or taking a known part from the whole when a part is unknown.

activities.title: Missing-number and word-problem practice set
steps: Fill in equations with the unknown in different positions, e.g. 7 = ▢ − 9, ▢ + 5 = 12, 12 − ▢ = 8.
Answer word problems with picture support where the unknown is the result, change or start.
Mark which problems were 'find the start' problems rather than 'find what's left'.
activities.insight: Problems with the unknown in varied positions require the same modelling reasoning; recognising the structure matters more than the keyword.

checkQuestion: Solve these — you can use counters. (1) I have 12 sweets and eat 4 — how many are left? (2) There were some cars; 5 drive away and 7 are left — how many were there at the start? (3) Fill the box: 7 = ▢ − 9.
